sourceNotes: Seeded from BFS roleplay performance indicators and finance cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: BFS event flavor, then this event's own instructional areas, then the rest of the finance cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: A measure of gain or benefit compared with the cost of an investment.
terms.whyItMatters: ROI helps justify business spending.

terms.definition: The dollar ceiling a revolving lender will actually advance, recomputed each month as eligible receivables times their advance rate plus eligible inventory times its own, after ineligibles such as invoices over 90 days, foreign accounts and affiliate sales are struck out.
terms.whyItMatters: A BFS roleplay asking how much a distributor may draw this month is answered by rebuilding this schedule line by line, not by quoting the facility's face amount.

terms.definition: The percentage of a pledged asset's book value a lender is willing to lend against — commonly 80 to 85% on eligible receivables but only 40 to 50% on inventory, because expected recovery in a liquidation differs sharply by asset class.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you a collateral schedule and ask for available credit; each asset class must be multiplied by its own rate rather than by one blended percentage.

terms.definition: A drawn balance sitting above what the collateral formula supports, allowed only by written lender consent and normally carried at a penalty rate with a dated cure schedule rather than left open-ended.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay client has drawn $2.1M against a $1.9M base, the judge wants the cure plan — pay down, pledge more collateral, or negotiate a temporary block — with the deadline attached.

terms.definition: Cash available for debt service divided by the year's scheduled principal plus interest; commercial lenders generally demand at least 1.25x, so $125,000 of operating cash flow is needed to support $100,000 of annual payments.
terms.whyItMatters: Nearly every commercial lending roleplay turns on whether the borrower still clears the bank's 1.25x floor once the proposed new note is added to the existing payments.

terms.definition: Earnings before interest and taxes plus lease and rent expense, divided by interest plus those leases plus required principal — a harder test than interest coverage because it counts every obligation a company cannot postpone.
terms.whyItMatters: A franchise or restaurant borrower with heavy rent can pass interest coverage and still fail this covenant, and exam questions use that gap on purpose.

terms.definition: Total funded debt measured against one year of operating cash earnings and quoted as a multiple; middle-market credit agreements typically cap it near 3.0x and step the limit down as the loan amortizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a balance sheet and an income statement, a competitor must state whether a proposed $2M draw breaches the leverage cap before recommending the deal at all.

terms.definition: The cushion between where a borrower's tested ratio stands today and the level the credit agreement actually requires, usually expressed as the percentage earnings could fall before a breach occurs.
terms.whyItMatters: A treasury roleplay asking whether the firm can absorb one slow quarter is answered as a headroom number, not by restating what the covenant says.

terms.definition: Loan language letting a lender refuse to fund or accelerate the balance when the borrower's condition worsens significantly; courts read it narrowly and require a durationally significant decline, not a single disappointing quarter.
terms.whyItMatters: Cases about a bank walking away from a signed commitment mid-deal hinge entirely on whether the downturn is severe and lasting enough to trigger this clause.

terms.definition: The one-page public filing that perfects a lender's security interest in business collateral; priority runs first-to-file rather than first-to-lend, and the filing lapses after five years unless a continuation is filed in time.
terms.whyItMatters: A case asking why the second bank to lend got paid first is answered by comparing filing dates, and the five-year lapse is a favorite detail on the finance exam.

terms.definition: A contract in which one creditor agrees to be paid only after another is made whole, rearranging repayment priority by consent rather than by the order in which liens happened to be filed.
terms.whyItMatters: When a bank insists the owner's shareholder loan stand behind the new term debt before closing, the roleplay is asking for this document by name.

terms.definition: An annual charge, usually 25 to 50 basis points, assessed on the undrawn portion of a committed line — so a $5M facility drawn at $1M costs $10,000 a year at 25 bp even if nothing further is borrowed.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors are asked to weigh an oversized line's carrying cost against the flexibility it buys, and the answer is that arithmetic rather than a judgment call.

terms.definition: A credit-agreement mechanic forcing a stated share of leftover annual cash — often 50%, stepping down to 25% once leverage falls below a set multiple — into early repayment of the term loan.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking why a profitable client cannot self-fund an expansion usually has this clause buried in the loan documents, capturing the cash before management sees it.

terms.definition: Average receivables divided by credit sales and multiplied by the days in the period; 45 days against 30-day terms means customers run 15 days late and the seller is financing that gap out of its own line.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash-flow cases ask you to convert a collection delay into dollars tied up, and this figure has to be computed before the financing cost can be quoted.

terms.definition: Average payables divided by cost of goods sold times the period's days — how long a firm holds its suppliers' money, and the only leg of the cash cycle that shrinks the funding gap when it gets longer.
terms.whyItMatters: A judge will test whether stretching suppliers from 30 to 45 days is free financing or a forfeited early-payment discount that costs more than the bank line would.

terms.definition: The annualized price of skipping an early-payment discount: the discount divided by the amount still due, times 365 over the extra days of credit taken — terms of 2/10 net 30 work out near 37% a year.
terms.whyItMatters: Handed 2/10 net 30 terms and a 9% line of credit, a competitor must recommend borrowing to take the discount, and the 37% figure is the proof the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: A minimum deposit the borrower must leave idle at the lending bank; because that money cannot be spent, it raises the true cost — $100,000 borrowed at 8% with $20,000 frozen is really 10% on the $80,000 usable.
terms.whyItMatters: Loan-comparison items hide the lower stated rate behind this requirement, and the effective-rate calculation is what separates placing competitors from the rest.

terms.definition: A disbursement account funded only at the moment checks or ACH debits present, pulling exactly the amount cleared from a master concentration account so no idle cash is stranded in branch or division accounts.
terms.whyItMatters: Treasury roleplays about a multi-location retailer holding buffer cash in twelve separate accounts are asking for this structure and the interest it frees up.

terms.definition: Selling receivables outright so the buyer absorbs the loss when an account debtor fails financially; the fee runs above a recourse sale precisely because credit risk, not merely collection effort, changes hands.
terms.whyItMatters: A client worried about one large customer's solvency needs this distinction, plus the reminder that a dispute over the goods themselves still bounces the invoice back to the seller.

terms.definition: A buyer-arranged program where the buyer's bank pays approved supplier invoices early at a discount priced off the buyer's stronger credit rating, letting the buyer keep long terms while suppliers still collect in days.
terms.whyItMatters: Cases about a small vendor squeezed by a national retailer's 90-day terms are solved with this program, not with an ordinary factoring line the vendor could never price as cheaply.

terms.definition: Credit memos, returns, allowances and write-offs measured against gross sales; every point above roughly 5% tells an asset-based lender a dollar of invoice will not collect as a dollar, and the advance rate is trimmed to match.
terms.whyItMatters: When a lender cuts availability even though sales are growing, this ratio is the reason, and a competitor has to be able to name it and compute it from the sales journal.

terms.definition: A bank's written promise to pay a beneficiary only if the applicant defaults on some underlying obligation — a backstop expected never to be drawn, unlike a commercial credit that is the ordinary way a shipment gets paid.
terms.whyItMatters: Supplier and contract roleplays ask which instrument to offer a nervous counterparty, and drawing that line between backstop and payment mechanism is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Dun & Bradstreet's 1-to-100 payment index built from reported trade experiences and weighted by dollar size; 80 means invoices are paid on terms, 70 means roughly 15 days slow, and 50 means about 30 days slow.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier deciding whether to grant $50,000 of open terms reads these thresholds, and exam items pair the score with a personal credit score to test which one applies to a business.

terms.definition: The lender's evaluation frame — character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions — in which capacity means measured repayment cash flow and capital means the owner's own money already at risk, not net worth generally.
terms.whyItMatters: Loan-interview roleplays are scored on covering all five in order, and most competitors blur capital into collateral and lose the point outright.

terms.definition: Borrowing sized and priced off the liquidation value of receivables and inventory instead of off historical earnings, which is why the borrower reports collateral continuously and the lender monitors it between statements.
terms.whyItMatters: A fast-growing but not yet profitable client is the classic case where this beats a cash-flow term loan, and the roleplay expects that reasoning stated aloud.

terms.definition: A committed line a business may draw, repay and redraw up to a ceiling through its term, charging interest on the drawn balance and a fee on the rest — built for seasonal swings, not for buying equipment.
terms.whyItMatters: Matching the instrument to the need is a standard exam item: this covers the working-capital gap while a term loan covers the delivery truck.

terms.definition: The written analysis a loan officer carries to committee — borrower history, primary and secondary repayment sources ranked, collateral position and the recommended structure — not the credit note issued against a customer invoice.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask you to present the deal internally are asking for this document's structure spoken out loud, in that order.

terms.definition: A supplier's report on how an applicant business has actually paid — highest credit extended, current balance, amounts past due — gathered directly or through a bureau before open terms are approved.
terms.whyItMatters: A credit-department roleplay that grants terms without pulling two or three of these loses points for skipping verification, however good the financials look.

terms.definition: The total amount, including interest and fees, paid to borrow money.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing the true cost of credit lets competitors judge whether borrowing is worthwhile.

terms.definition: The line of authority defining who reports to whom in an organization.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing when and how to escalate is a frequent judgment point in roleplays.

terms.definition: Tangible products in limited supply that must be produced and purchased.
terms.whyItMatters: Distinguishing goods from services underlies every business model.

terms.definition: A document a seller issues to request payment for goods or services provided.
terms.whyItMatters: Invoices drive accounts-receivable timing and payment terms.

terms.definition: The principle that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future because it can earn a return.
terms.whyItMatters: This concept justifies interest, discounting, and why saving early beats saving late.

terms.definition: Credential a private board grants after a psychometrically validated exam and keeps alive through periodic recertification, evidencing tested competence rather than legal permission. A certificate of completion is the near-neighbor that fools students: it is awarded merely for finishing a course, is never re-earned, and no board can revoke it.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on career-advancement resources ask which credential an employer will actually pay for; the answer is the one with an exam and a renewal cycle behind it.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by the required reserve ratio, and caps how far one new deposit can expand the money supply: at a 10% reserve ratio the multiplier is 10, so $1,000 of fresh reserves can support up to $10,000 of deposits. Cash held outside banks and excess reserves both shrink the real-world figure below the formula.
terms.whyItMatters: Macro items that hand you a reserve ratio and a deposit want this reciprocal computed, and the deposit-expansion number is graded, not the explanation of lending.

terms.definition: Current assets minus current liabilities — a measure of short-term financial health.
terms.whyItMatters: Working capital shows whether a business can cover immediate obligations.

terms.definition: The total amount of tax a person or business legally owes to the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax liabilities affect take-home income and the real return on financial decisions.

terms.definition: An orderly, methodical approach to tasks and decisions that follows a logical structure.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges favor structured reasoning over a scattered approach.

terms.definition: How many times the average dollar is spent on final goods and services in a year, computed as nominal GDP divided by the money supply. It is the V in the equation of exchange MV = PQ, so when V is stable, growth in the money supply passes straight through into higher prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation items that ask why a large increase in the money supply did not produce proportional price increases are asking the competitor to reason about a fall in this ratio.

terms.definition: Recording revenue or expense when it is incurred, not when cash changes hands.
terms.whyItMatters: Accrual accounting reveals true profitability beyond the cash view.

terms.definition: The yearly cost of borrowing stated as a percentage that folds in interest plus required fees, so two loans quoted at the same interest rate can carry different borrowing costs.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-of-credit questions on the finance exam ask which loan is cheaper, and the answer is the one with the lower APR, not the lower nominal interest rate.

terms.definition: Standard measure of non-degree instruction in which one unit equals 10 contact hours of participation in an accredited program, so a two-day 16-hour seminar earns 1.6 units. A college credit hour is a different currency entirely — roughly 15 contact hours across a semester — and licensing boards rarely convert one into the other.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked on the exam to price a training plan against a 40-hour renewal requirement, a competitor has to convert seminar hours into units before the budget makes sense.

terms.definition: The inputs — land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship — used to produce goods and services.
terms.whyItMatters: Managing limited resources is central to operations and strategy.

terms.definition: Money a business owes to suppliers for goods or services already received.
terms.whyItMatters: Payables shape the cash position competitors must manage.

terms.definition: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce overall risk.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversification is the standard answer to lowering investment risk in finance events.

terms.definition: Building and maintaining relationships with professionals to exchange knowledge and opportunity.
terms.whyItMatters: Networking is essential for discovering and advancing career opportunities.

terms.definition: The relationship stating that the real interest rate equals the nominal rate minus expected inflation, so a savings account paying 7% during 5% inflation earns only about 2% in purchasing power — and a 3% account during 4% inflation loses money in real terms even though the balance grows.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal-finance or economics item that gives a stated rate and an inflation rate is asking for the real return; answering with the posted nominal rate is the standard miss.

terms.definition: A list of all ledger accounts and balances used to check that debits equal credits.
terms.whyItMatters: Trial balances verify the accuracy of financial records in case work.

terms.definition: What a deposit actually earns over a year once compounding is counted, which is why a savings account paying 5% compounded monthly returns more than 5%.
terms.whyItMatters: A savings-comparison roleplay hands the competitor two accounts with the same stated rate but different compounding periods; APY is the only figure that ranks them.

terms.definition: Licensing threshold most states impose on CPA candidates: 150 semester hours of college credit — 30 beyond the 120 a bachelor's degree typically carries — plus all four sections of the Uniform CPA Exam and a year of supervised experience. Several states now allow a bachelor's degree plus two years of experience as an alternate route to the same license.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting-designations roleplay asks what a college junior must still complete before licensure; the answer is a credit count and an exam, not a job offer.

terms.definition: Federal coverage of $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — so a couple's joint account is insured separately from each spouse's individual account, and the cap applies per institution rather than per branch or per account number.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a client asks whether their savings are safe after a bank failure is scored on stating the dollar cap and the per-depositor, per-bank, per-category structure.

terms.definition: The dollar gap between inventory valued under FIFO and the same inventory valued under LIFO — FIFO inventory minus LIFO inventory — disclosed in the notes so a reader can restate a LIFO firm's inventory and cost of goods sold onto a FIFO basis before comparing it with anyone else.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand you a footnote figure and ask you to compare two competitors' inventory when one uses LIFO and one uses FIFO; the comparison means nothing until the reserve is added back.

terms.definition: Total monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income, the figure a lender uses to decide how much more a borrower can carry.
terms.whyItMatters: Loan-approval scenarios turn on this number, and competitors are expected to compute it from a client's payment list rather than judge the debt total by feel.

terms.definition: The advancement path within an organization based on skills, performance, and leadership.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding progression guides career decisions in higher-level scenarios.

terms.definition: Occurs when short-term Treasury yields sit above long-term ones — the 10-year minus 2-year spread turns negative — because investors expect rate cuts and weaker growth ahead. It has preceded every U.S. recession since the 1950s, typically by six to twenty-four months, which is why it is treated as a leading signal rather than a description of current conditions.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle items that hand you bond yields at several maturities are asking what the shape of the curve forecasts, not what the economy is doing today.

terms.definition: Money owed to a business by customers for goods or services already delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: Receivables affect cash flow timing and collection decisions.

terms.definition: An institution such as a bank, credit union, or brokerage that offers money-management products.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right provider is a recurring judgment in personal-finance scenarios.

terms.definition: Investment credential awarded after passing three sequential exams, each historically about six hours, and documenting 4,000 hours of qualified work experience earned over a minimum of 36 months. It certifies analytical competence only: unlike a CPA license it grants no legal authority to audit financial statements or sign a tax return.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-finance roleplay explaining designations to an intern, the tested contrast is that this one signals analysis while the CPA license signals attest authority.

terms.definition: The output produced per unit of input, such as per worker or per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: Higher productivity lowers cost and builds competitive advantage.

terms.definition: A write-down rule under ASC 330: inventory carried at historical cost must be reduced to replacement cost when that is lower, but never above net realizable value — selling price minus completion and disposal costs — nor below that ceiling minus a normal profit margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges ask what to do about obsolete stock still on the books at full cost; the answer is the mandatory write-down and the loss it forces onto this period's income statement.

terms.definition: Balances owed divided by total available revolving credit, weighted heavily in a credit score and generally kept under 30% to avoid a penalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Credit-score advising roleplays reward the competitor who tells a client to pay down balances or raise a limit instead of closing an unused card.

terms.definition: Two-part credential in financial planning, analysis and strategic decision support, requiring a bachelor's degree, two years of management-accounting experience, and 30 continuing hours a year of which 2 must be ethics. It is built for internal decision support, whereas the CPA license exists for the external attest work a CMA holder may not sign.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay asking which credential fits a cost-analyst career path needs this internal-versus-external split stated with its hour requirement.

terms.definition: The share of each ADDITIONAL dollar of after-tax income a household spends rather than saves, computed as the change in consumption divided by the change in income. It always pairs with the marginal propensity to save, and the two sum to 1 — so an MPC of 0.75 implies an MPS of 0.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give a household's income increase and its spending increase want this ratio, which then feeds the spending multiplier; using average spending out of total income instead of the change is the classic error.

terms.definition: An estimate of ending inventory made without a physical count: multiply net sales by the historical gross-profit percentage to approximate cost of goods sold, then subtract that from the cost of goods available for sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Insurance-claim and interim-statement questions give you sales figures and a prior-year margin but no count, and this is the only route to an inventory number a judge will accept.

terms.definition: A financial statement reporting the cash flowing into and out of a business over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash flow reveals whether a business can pay its bills even when it reports a profit.

terms.definition: State-granted legal permission to perform work that is illegal without it — signing an audit opinion, selling securities, practicing law. A voluntary certification is issued by a private association instead, so losing it costs you the letters after your name but never the legal right to keep working.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay that asks what a new hire may and may not sign turns on this line: an unlicensed staff accountant can prepare the workpapers but cannot issue the opinion.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by (1 − MPC), so an economy whose households spend 80 cents of each extra dollar turns $10 billion of new government purchases into as much as $50 billion of added output. The tax multiplier is always smaller, because the first dollar of a tax cut is partly saved before any of it is spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A macro item that supplies an MPC and a spending figure is asking for this computation; the tax-cut version of the same question uses a smaller multiplier and is where competitors lose points.

terms.definition: The difference between a budgeted amount and the actual amount spent or earned.
terms.whyItMatters: Variances flag where a plan and reality diverge, prompting corrective action.

terms.definition: A shortcut that estimates how many years an investment takes to double by dividing 72 by the annual percentage return.
terms.whyItMatters: Investing roleplays reward a competitor who can tell a client on the spot that 8% doubles their money in about nine years.

terms.definition: FINRA registration permitting an individual to sell general securities to the public, earned by passing the Securities Industry Essentials exam plus a top-off exam and requiring sponsorship by a member firm — a candidate cannot even sit for it unaffiliated. Charging a fee for advice rather than selling products requires a Series 65 or 66 instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services roleplay that asks what a new advisor may do on day one hinges on which registration is in place and who sponsored it.

terms.definition: Totals a nation's output as C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption plus business investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Imports are SUBTRACTED because they were produced abroad but already counted inside C, I and G, which is why a widening trade deficit mechanically lowers the measured figure.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP items hand you four spending categories and expect the sum with imports netted out; adding imports in, or counting government transfer payments as G, are the two ways competitors miss it.

terms.definition: Delivery terms placing title and risk of loss with the buyer the moment a carrier takes the goods, so the buyer adds the freight to inventory cost and reports goods still in transit at period end — the mirror of FOB destination, where the seller keeps both title and freight until delivery.
terms.whyItMatters: Cutoff questions ask which company reports a shipment sitting on a truck on December 31, and the answer turns entirely on which of the two terms the invoice names.

terms.definition: The rate applied to the next dollar earned, which is the top bracket a taxpayer reaches rather than the rate paid on all of their income.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-liability items test whether a raise into a higher bracket taxes the whole salary at the new rate — it does not, only the dollars above the bracket line.

terms.definition: Renewal credit a credentialed professional must earn on a fixed cycle to keep the credential active — most state boards require a CPA to report 120 hours across a rolling three-year period with a 20-hour annual floor plus a mandated ethics course, and unused hours lapse rather than carry forward. Unlike a degree, it has no completion point.
terms.whyItMatters: The finance roleplay that asks how an accountant stays qualified year to year wants the cycle and the hour count, not a sentence about lifelong learning.

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: A bad-debt estimate built from a schedule that sorts every customer balance by days past due and applies a rising uncollectible rate to each bucket, targeting the ENDING allowance balance — unlike the percentage-of-sales approach, which computes the period's expense straight from revenue and ignores whatever already sits in the allowance.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam gives you an aging schedule plus an existing allowance balance, and the adjusting entry is the difference between them, not the computed total.

terms.definition: A financial statement showing a business's assets, liabilities, and equity at a single point in time.
terms.whyItMatters: The balance sheet is where competitors read financial position and solvency.

terms.definition: Freedom from any relationship that would let a firm review its own work: Sarbanes-Oxley bars nine categories of non-audit service for an audit client, forces the lead partner off the engagement after five years, and imposes a one-year cooling-off period before an auditor may join that client as CFO or controller. Objectivity is a mindset; this is the enforceable rule set.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay in which the audit firm is offered the client's bookkeeping work is decided by these prohibitions, not by whether the team feels unbiased.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: A detail file holding one account per customer, vendor, or asset, whose balances must total exactly to the single control account carrying that category in the general ledger — the general ledger holds the summary figure that reaches the statements, this holds the per-name detail that supports it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking which specific customers owe the overdue balance is answered from this ledger; the trial balance shows only one combined receivable line.

terms.definition: Total tax paid divided by total income, always lower than the top bracket a taxpayer falls in because earlier dollars were taxed at lower rates.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam item gives income and tax owed and asks for the rate actually paid; answering with the bracket rate is the trap.

terms.definition: Member-governed body that publishes a code of ethics, administers credentialing exams and sets practice standards for a field — the AICPA for accountants, SHRM for HR professionals. A labor union may cover overlapping workers but bargains collectively over wages and conditions; an association negotiates nothing and its only sanction is revoking the credential.
terms.whyItMatters: The accounting roleplay that asks what a professional organization does for a member is scored on services and enforcement, and confusing it with a union loses the item.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: Recording a bad debt only when one specific account is judged worthless, charging it to expense in that later period — required on U.S. tax returns but unacceptable under GAAP for material amounts, because it breaks the match between the expense and the revenue that created the receivable, which the allowance method preserves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why a small firm's books disagree with its tax return, and the timing split between these two methods is the reason.

terms.definition: A financial statement showing revenue, expenses, and profit over a period of time.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the primary tool for judging whether operations are profitable.

terms.definition: Duty a broker-dealer owes to recommend products that fit a customer's stated objectives, raised in 2020 to a best-interest obligation requiring conflicts to be disclosed. It still stops short of the fiduciary standard a registered investment adviser owes under the Advisers Act of 1940, where the client's interest comes first continuously, not only at the moment of a recommendation.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-advising roleplay about recommending a higher-commission fund turns on which of the two duties the professional is actually held to.

terms.definition: The percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it.
terms.whyItMatters: It signals economic health and shapes consumer spending and hiring.

terms.definition: Cost minus salvage value, divided by total estimated lifetime output, multiplied by the units actually produced this period — expense tracks usage rather than the passage of time, so a machine that sat idle all year records none at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a press rated for 500,000 impressions and 40,000 run this year, the exam expects the per-unit rate, not the straight-line annual amount.

terms.definition: An amount subtracted directly from tax owed, so it is worth its full face value — unlike a deduction, which only reduces the income the tax is figured on.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a $1,000 credit with a $1,000 deduction and ask which saves more; the credit does, by the taxpayer's bracket rate.

terms.definition: Statement of the principles a profession owes the public, enforced by a licensing or membership board that can suspend or revoke the credential itself. A code of conduct is narrower and employer-issued: it lists prohibited acts and is enforced through progressive discipline up to termination, which ends the job but leaves the right to practice intact.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where an employee follows company policy yet violates a professional standard requires naming which body can act and what each can take away.

terms.definition: The empirical rule that each percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate costs roughly 2% of potential real GDP, so an economy running 3 points above that rate is producing about 6% less than its capacity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give an actual unemployment rate and a natural rate and ask what output is being lost are solved with this two-to-one ratio rather than by describing the recession in words.

terms.definition: Cash the company has already recorded and sent to the bank that the bank has not yet posted, so it is ADDED to the bank side of a reconciliation — the opposite column from an outstanding check, which is also unposted by the bank but subtracted there, and neither one requires a journal entry on the books.
terms.whyItMatters: Reconciliation items are scored on which column they adjust and whether an entry is needed, and this pair is the one candidates reverse most often.

terms.definition: Profit from selling an asset for more than its purchase price, taxable only once the sale happens and taxed at a lower rate when the asset was held over a year.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios ask whether a client owes tax on a stock that has risen in value; unrealized gains are not taxed until sold.

terms.definition: Statutory shield for an employee who reports suspected fraud: Sarbanes-Oxley gives a retaliation complaint 180 days to reach OSHA, while Dodd-Frank pays an SEC tipster 10% to 30% of sanctions when the recovery exceeds $1 million. Reporting internally first preserves the retaliation claim but is not a precondition of the SEC award.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-ethics roleplay about a coworker's falsified expense reports, the graded answer names the channel and the filing window, not just 'tell someone'.

terms.definition: The labor force — everyone employed or actively searching within the last four weeks — divided by the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over, times 100. It can fall at the same time as the unemployment rate, because a discouraged worker who stops searching leaves the numerator and the jobless count simultaneously.
terms.whyItMatters: Items pair a falling unemployment rate with a falling participation rate and ask whether the labor market really improved; the arithmetic of who leaves the labor force is what settles it.

terms.definition: The depreciation schedule the Internal Revenue Code requires on tax returns, assigning each asset class a fixed recovery period and IRS table percentage under a half-year or mid-quarter convention — deliberately faster than the straight-line figure the same asset carries on the GAAP books, which is exactly what creates a deferred tax liability.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions asking why book income and taxable income differ for the same delivery truck are answered by naming this schedule and its accelerated front-loading.

terms.definition: How easily an asset can be converted to cash without losing much value.
terms.whyItMatters: Liquidity explains why a profitable business can still run short of cash.

terms.definition: Stretch of the calendar when insiders may not trade their own company's stock, typically closing two to four weeks before quarter-end and reopening one to two full trading days after earnings are released. A Rule 10b5-1 plan is the only clean way around it: trades are pre-scheduled and, under the 2023 amendments, cannot begin for at least 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay in which an employee wants to sell vested shares the week before an earnings release is answered by the window, not by intent.

terms.definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower OPPORTUNITY cost than a trading partner, which is what makes trade mutually profitable even when one country is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage — simply making more per hour of input — does not by itself establish any reason to trade.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade items give a two-country, two-good output table and ask who should specialize in what; the answer comes from the opportunity-cost ratios, not from whichever column of raw output is larger.

terms.definition: A permanent write-down under ASC 360: when events suggest a long-lived asset will not recover its carrying amount, that amount is first compared with the undiscounted future cash flows the asset will generate, and only if it fails that recoverability test is it written down to fair value — a one-time loss, not the periodic allocation depreciation performs.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay scenarios about a shuttered plant still carried at cost test whether you know the write-down is required rather than optional.

terms.definition: Matching a checkbook or ledger against a bank statement by adjusting both sides — outstanding checks and deposits in transit on the bank's, fees and interest on the depositor's.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam item gives a statement balance and a book balance and asks for the true cash figure; only adjusting one side gets it wrong.

terms.definition: Flat daily travel allowance that substitutes for itemized receipts — the federal standard for the continental U.S. runs near $110 for lodging plus $68 for meals and incidentals, with the first and last travel days paid at 75% of the meal portion. Anything paid above the published rate becomes taxable wages to the traveler.
terms.whyItMatters: A hospitality or sales roleplay budgeting a three-day trip needs the arithmetic: two full days at the meal rate plus two partial days at three quarters of it.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP is the standard gauge of economic health competitors reference.

terms.definition: A company's own shares bought back and held rather than retired, carried at repurchase cost as a NEGATIVE item within stockholders' equity and never as an asset. It draws no dividend and casts no vote, which is precisely why issued shares and outstanding shares stop being the same number once a buyback occurs.
terms.whyItMatters: Earnings-per-share questions require the outstanding share count, and a buyback is the event that pulls the two counts apart.

terms.definition: Paying a loan off through fixed installments split between interest and principal, with the interest share largest at the start and shrinking every payment.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why an early mortgage payment barely reduces the balance; the amortization split is the reason, not a fee.

terms.definition: Dollar ceiling below which accepting a business courtesy is not treated as influence — federal ethics rules cap it at $20 per occasion and $50 per source per year, and many corporate policies copy those figures. Above the line the item must be refused, returned, or reported, and splitting one gift across two occasions is itself the violation.
terms.whyItMatters: A purchasing roleplay where a vendor sends playoff tickets is scored on whether the competitor applies the stated dollar limit and the reporting step.

terms.definition: The complete record of a nation's transactions with the rest of the world — the current account of goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts — which sums to zero by construction, since a current-account deficit is financed by an offsetting inflow of capital. The balance of trade is only the goods-and-services slice of the current account.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items ask what a persistent trade deficit implies; the correct answer follows the offsetting capital inflow rather than treating the deficit as unfunded loss.

terms.definition: The excess of a purchase price over the fair value of the identifiable net assets acquired in a business combination — recognizable only through an acquisition, never for internally built reputation — and under ASC 350 never amortized, only tested for impairment at least annually.
terms.whyItMatters: Balance-sheet questions following an acquisition ask what the large intangible line actually represents and why it does not depreciate like equipment.

terms.definition: Current assets divided by current liabilities, the standard test of whether a business can cover what it owes within the next twelve months.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand over a balance sheet and ask whether the firm can meet short-term obligations; a ratio under 1.0 is the answer that says no.

terms.definition: Post-employment restriction barring a departing worker from joining a competitor for a stated period and geography, commonly 6 to 12 months. Enforceability is a state question — California voids them outright and several states exempt hourly workers below a wage threshold — and a court will usually narrow an unreasonable radius rather than rewrite the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay advising an employee who has an offer from a rival turns on this clause's scope and on whether the state will enforce it at all.

terms.definition: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same in both countries: if a burger is $5 in the U.S. and £4 in Britain, the implied rate is $1.25 per pound, and a market rate of $1.60 says the pound is overvalued. Trade barriers and non-traded services keep real rates from converging to it.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items give two local prices for one product and ask what the exchange rate implies, or ask why a salary converts to very different living standards in two countries.

terms.definition: An outlay charged to expense in the period incurred because it only maintains an asset's existing capacity — routine repairs, servicing, replacement parts — as opposed to a capital expenditure, which extends useful life or output and is therefore added to the asset account and depreciated across the years it benefits.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you an oil-change bill and an engine-rebuild bill on the same truck and ask which one hits this year's income statement in full.

terms.definition: Current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities — the stricter liquidity test, because inventory may not convert to cash in time to pay a bill.
terms.whyItMatters: A retailer with a healthy current ratio and a weak quick ratio is the classic exam case, and the difference is inventory the business cannot sell fast.

terms.definition: Reimbursement arrangement that keeps expense payments out of taxable wages, valid only when the expense has a business connection, is substantiated with receipts within 60 days, and any excess advance is returned within 120 days. Miss any one of the three and the arrangement is non-accountable, so every reimbursed dollar is added to the W-2 and taxed as pay.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on a sales rep who never turns in travel receipts is really asking why the reimbursement showed up as taxable income.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: The private, non-governmental body that writes U.S. GAAP and publishes it as the Accounting Standards Codification, operating under SEC oversight rather than by direct statute — distinct from the International Accounting Standards Board, which issues IFRS for most of the rest of the world.
terms.whyItMatters: Regulation questions ask who actually sets the rules a U.S. company must follow, and the answer is a standard-setting board, not a government agency.

terms.definition: A tax structure whose rate rises as income rises, taxing each band of income at its own rate — the opposite of a regressive tax that takes a larger share from lower earners.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-structure questions ask competitors to classify income tax, sales tax and payroll tax, and sales tax is regressive despite its single rate.

terms.definition: Withholding certificate an employee files so the employer deducts the right federal income tax; the 2020 redesign dropped allowances for a five-step worksheet stated in dollars, including $2,000 per qualifying child. It is not Form I-9, which proves work authorization within three business days of hire, nor Form W-9, which an independent contractor files instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A first-day onboarding roleplay is scored on knowing which of the three forms does what, since a competitor who names the wrong one has the new hire unpaid or unauthorized.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: A postponement entry for cash that has already changed hands but has not yet been earned or used up — unearned revenue and prepaid assets sit on the balance sheet until the service is delivered or the benefit consumed — the exact reverse of an accrual, where the revenue or expense is recognized first and the cash follows later.
terms.whyItMatters: Adjusting-entry questions are sorted by deciding which side of this split a transaction falls on before any journal entry gets written.

terms.definition: Total liabilities divided by owner's equity, showing how much of the business is financed by lenders rather than owners and how exposed it is to a downturn.
terms.whyItMatters: Financing scenarios ask whether a firm can take on another loan, and a high ratio is the reason a lender says no.

terms.definition: Narrower post-employment restriction that lets a departing worker take any job but forbids contacting the former employer's customers or recruiting its staff, usually for 12 to 24 months. Because it limits whom you may approach rather than where you may work, courts enforce it in states that will not enforce a non-compete at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay about a rep who leaves and calls his old book of business is decided by this clause, not by the broader competition ban.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: A fund fixed at a set dollar amount where every disbursement must be backed by a receipt, so vouchers plus remaining cash always equal that fixed total and replenishment is written for exactly what was spent — unlike a fluctuating fund, topped up in round sums, where a shortage simply disappears into the next refill.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash-control roleplays ask how a small office can hand out cash all week and still detect a missing twenty dollars; the fixed balance is what makes the shortage visible.

terms.definition: The payroll deduction funding Social Security and Medicare, taken at a fixed percentage of wages and matched dollar for dollar by the employer.
terms.whyItMatters: Pay-stub interpretation items ask why gross pay minus income tax still does not equal take-home pay, and FICA is the missing line.

terms.definition: State or city rule requiring an employer to publish a good-faith salary range inside the job posting itself, as Colorado's Equal Pay for Equal Work Act and New York City's Local Law 32 do. It attacks the gap at the offer stage, whereas the Equal Pay Act of 1963 works after the fact by requiring equal pay for substantially equal work.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay preparing a competitor to negotiate an offer changes completely when the posted range is public, because the anchor is set before the conversation.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: A potential obligation that depends on some future event — a pending lawsuit, a warranty claim, a loan guarantee. Under ASC 450 it is accrued as both expense and liability only when the loss is probable AND reasonably estimable; when it is merely reasonably possible it is disclosed in the notes and stays off the balance sheet entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a suit filed in November and ask whether it changes the statements or only the footnotes, and the two-condition test decides it.

terms.definition: Net income divided by owner's equity, measuring profit generated per dollar the owners have invested rather than per dollar of sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items compare two firms with equal profits and different equity bases; the one earning more per invested dollar wins.

terms.definition: Employment clause transferring to the employer any invention conceived during the job, reaching further than copyright's work-made-for-hire rule because it also captures patents. Statutes such as California Labor Code section 2870 carve out inventions developed entirely on the worker's own time, without company equipment or trade secrets, and unrelated to the employer's business.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay about a side project built after hours is scored on whether the competitor can state the carve-out's three conditions.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: The IASB-issued reporting framework used across most non-U.S. markets. It is principles-based where U.S. GAAP is rules-based, bans LIFO outright, permits upward revaluation of fixed assets to fair value, and allows reversal of a prior inventory write-down — three things GAAP forbids.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions about a firm that reports in two markets test whether you can name a specific divergence rather than just assert that the frameworks differ.

terms.definition: Net income available to common shareholders divided by shares outstanding, the per-share figure that lets companies of different sizes be compared.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios quote it as the headline number, and a competitor is expected to know a buyback raises it without any change in profit.

terms.definition: Paid notice period during which a resigning employee stays on payroll but is kept away from the office, from clients and from starting at a competitor, commonly one to six months. It is enforceable in places that void a bare non-compete precisely because the employer keeps paying — the restraint is bought rather than merely imposed.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay advising a senior manager on a competitor's offer must separate this paid restriction from an unpaid non-compete, because only one keeps income flowing.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: Tax that will come due in later years because a temporary timing difference — most often faster depreciation on the return than on the books — held taxable income below book income now. It reverses in future periods, unlike a permanent difference such as a government fine, which never reverses and creates no such account.
terms.whyItMatters: Balance-sheet questions ask why a profitable firm reports a tax obligation far larger than the check it actually wrote to the IRS this year.

terms.definition: A retirement account whose contributions escape tax now and whose withdrawals are taxed later, trading a deduction today for taxable income in retirement.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement-planning roleplays turn on when the client wants the tax bill, which is the whole traditional-versus-Roth decision.

terms.definition: Department of Labor-registered training program pairing paid on-the-job hours — about 2,000 a year under a journey-worker mentor — with at least 144 hours of related classroom instruction and scheduled wage increases as each skill is certified. An internship carries no registered hour floor, no mentor requirement and no guaranteed wage progression.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on ways to gain real work experience is scored on naming the structured, paid, credentialed route rather than only the summer internship.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: The portion of a stock issuance received above the arbitrary par amount — shares sold at $12 with a $1 par put $1 per share into the common stock account and the other $11 per share here — so only the two accounts read together show what investors actually contributed.
terms.whyItMatters: Equity-section questions give an issue price and a par value and expect the proceeds split correctly across both lines rather than dumped into one.

terms.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share, the number of dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual profit — a rough gauge of how much growth is priced in.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a client on whether a stock looks expensive in an investing roleplay turns on this multiple, not on the share price alone.

terms.definition: Employment term routing disputes to a private arbitrator instead of a court, waiving a jury and usually class treatment; the Federal Arbitration Act makes it binding and the award is nearly unappealable on the merits. The 2022 Ending Forced Arbitration Act carves out sexual assault and harassment claims, which an employee may still take to court.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay walking a new hire through an offer packet has to flag what this clause gives up, since signing happens on day one and matters years later.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: The oversight body created by the Sarbanes-Oxley Act to register, inspect, and discipline the firms that audit public companies and to set the standards those audits follow — replacing the profession's earlier self-regulation through the AICPA, which now writes standards only for private-company engagements.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and regulation questions ask what structurally changed for auditors after the accounting scandals, and the end of self-policing is the specific answer.

terms.definition: A retirement account funded with money already taxed, whose qualified withdrawals — contributions and growth alike — come out tax-free.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a young client in a retirement roleplay usually points here, because decades of growth escape tax when the current bracket is low.

terms.definition: Four-quadrant triage that sorts a task list on two separate axes, urgency and importance: important and urgent is handled now, important and not urgent is scheduled and is where career-building work lives, urgent and not important is delegated, and neither is dropped. The insight is that a loud task can rank last.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay handed a full inbox and one afternoon is scored on the quadrant each item lands in and the action that quadrant dictates.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: Something that happens between the balance-sheet date and the day statements are issued. ASC 855 splits them in two: if the underlying condition already existed at the balance-sheet date — a customer bankruptcy confirming a receivable was already bad — the statements are adjusted; if the condition arose afterward, such as a warehouse fire in January, it is disclosed only.
terms.whyItMatters: Year-end roleplays ask whether a January development changes December's reported numbers, and this recognized-versus-nonrecognized split is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Annual dividends per share divided by share price, stating income return as a percentage so a dividend stock can be compared against a savings rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A client asking for income rather than growth in a retirement roleplay is asking about this figure, which moves whenever the share price moves.

terms.definition: Sworn statement the CEO and CFO sign with every quarterly and annual report, affirming that it is accurate and that they evaluated the effectiveness of disclosure controls as of the period's end. Section 906 supplies the teeth: a knowing false certification carries fines up to $5 million and imprisonment up to 20 years.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay about pressure to delay recognizing an expense is answered by naming who personally signs for the numbers and what the penalty is.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: The threshold at which an omission or misstatement would change a reasonable user's decision. SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 99 rejects any pure size rule: a five-percent-of-income screen may flag items, but a tiny error that flips a loss into a profit, hides a broken loan covenant, or lifts a bonus over its target is material no matter how small the dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions ask whether a deliberate but tiny misstatement is acceptable, and the qualitative half of this standard is why the answer is no.

terms.definition: The sum of a project's future cash flows discounted back to today's dollars, minus its initial cost — positive means the project earns more than the required return.
terms.whyItMatters: Capital-investment items ask whether to buy the equipment, and the sign of this figure is the answer regardless of how large the raw cash flows look.

terms.definition: Allocation of professional growth into three ratios: 70% from challenging on-the-job assignments, 20% from developmental relationships such as coaching and feedback, and only 10% from formal courses. It reframes a development plan away from a training catalog and toward the stretch assignment that produces most of the learning.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay building a development plan for a high-potential employee loses points if the whole plan is a list of seminars.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: Choosing among permissible accounting options — timing a shipment, trimming a reserve, deferring maintenance — to steer reported income toward a target while staying technically inside GAAP. That technical legality is what separates it from outright fraud, and why the ethical question becomes one of intent and disclosure rather than rule-breaking.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics prompts describe a manager pushing December orders out the door to hit a quarterly number and ask whether anything wrong happened even though no rule was broken.

terms.definition: Investing a fixed amount on a fixed schedule regardless of price, which buys more shares when prices are low and lowers the average cost per share over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment roleplays ask how a client should handle a volatile market, and this is the answer that beats trying to time an entry point.

terms.definition: Worker excluded from federal overtime because the job clears both a salary-basis test and a duties test — at least $684 a week, which annualizes to $35,568, plus genuine executive, administrative or professional duties. A non-exempt worker, salaried or not, earns 1.5 times the regular rate beyond 40 hours in a week, and a job title alone never settles the classification.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on worker rights that gives an assistant manager a $700 weekly salary and 50 hours is testing both prongs of this test at once.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: The clean verdict an independent auditor issues when statements are fairly presented in all material respects — a conclusion about conformity with the reporting framework, not a guarantee of accuracy or solvency. It ranks above a qualified opinion, which carries one bounded exception, an adverse opinion, which says the statements are materially misstated, and a disclaimer, where the auditor could not gather enough evidence to conclude at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items quote an audit report and ask what a lender may safely conclude from that specific wording.

terms.definition: The percentage used to convert a future dollar into today's dollars; raising it lowers the present value of every future cash flow and can flip a project from worth doing to not.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the input that makes a net-present-value question answerable, and exam items test that a riskier project carries a higher one.

terms.definition: Inventory of the behaviors a role requires, each rated on a defined proficiency scale — commonly five levels from awareness to expert — with written behavioral anchors describing what each level looks like in practice. A job description lists duties and reporting lines; this states how well, which is what makes it scoreable.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asked to justify why one of two equally experienced candidates is ready for the role needs a scored scale, not an impression.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: The five-component model regulators and auditors use to evaluate controls — control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring — and the benchmark against which management's Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404 assessment is judged. It supplies the structure; any single safeguard, such as splitting custody from recordkeeping, sits inside just one of the five.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays asking a manager to evaluate a store's controls expect the five components as the outline of the answer, not a scattered list of fixes.

terms.definition: The yearly percentage of assets a fund charges to operate, deducted from returns automatically so the investor never sees a bill for it.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two funds with identical holdings in an investment scenario comes down to this figure, since it compounds against the client every year.

terms.definition: Warning an employer must send before rejecting an applicant because of a background-check report, enclosing a copy of the report and a summary of rights under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, then waiting a reasonable interval — five business days is the common practice — so the applicant can dispute an error before the final adverse-action notice issues.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring roleplay where a screening report shows a charge that belongs to someone else is scored on this two-notice sequence and the gap between them.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: A machine-readable tagging standard the SEC requires in filings, attaching a defined element to every reported figure so that one firm's net revenue line and another's total revenues line resolve to the same concept and load into an analyst's model without anyone rekeying them.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology questions ask how thousands of filings get screened automatically, and standardized tagging rather than a spreadsheet import is the answer.

terms.definition: The nominal return minus the inflation rate — what an investment actually gained in purchasing power, which can be negative while the account balance rises.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a 2% savings account with 3% inflation and ask whether the saver gained; the account grew and the money bought less.

terms.definition: Promise of company shares delivered on a vesting date and taxed as ordinary income on the full market value at vest — 400 shares vesting at $50 is $20,000 of W-2 wages whether or not a single share is sold. A stock option instead taxes the spread at exercise and is worth nothing while the price sits below the strike, which this grant never is.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two offers in a roleplay is impossible without valuing the equity: the exam wants shares times price times the vesting fraction, plus the tax hit at vest.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: A statistical regularity in naturally occurring figures: the leading digit is a 1 about 30% of the time and a 9 under 5% of the time, tapering logarithmically. Auditors run whole transaction files against that expected frequency because invented numbers cluster on middle digits and round amounts, which flags a batch for review rather than proving any single entry false.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about spotting fabricated entries want a specific analytic test run against the ledger, not a general claim that software catches fraud.

terms.definition: The total annualized return on a bond held to the end of its term, counting coupon payments plus any gain or loss between purchase price and face value.
terms.whyItMatters: A bond bought below face value returns more than its stated coupon rate, and this is the figure that shows it in an investment comparison.

terms.definition: Subtraction run one competency at a time — required proficiency minus current proficiency — with the resulting gaps ranked by size multiplied by how critical the competency is, so a 2-point gap on a critical skill outranks a 3-point gap on a peripheral one. Without the criticality weighting it degenerates into a list of everything someone cannot do.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on assessing your own interests and skills against an employer's expectations is really asking for this weighted subtraction.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.term: Indirect method of cash flow reporting
terms.definition: Building the operating section by starting from net income and reconciling it: add back non-cash charges such as depreciation, strip out gains and losses belonging to investing, then adjust for changes in current assets and liabilities. The direct method instead lists actual cash receipts and payments; both reach an identical operating total, and this one dominates practice because it reuses figures the books already carry.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash-flow questions show a profitable firm running short of cash, and this reconciliation is where the receivable and inventory buildup becomes visible.

terms.definition: What a sum invested today grows to by a stated date at a stated rate, computed forward with compounding rather than by adding equal yearly amounts.
terms.whyItMatters: Savings-goal items give a monthly deposit and a rate and ask what the account holds in ten years; straight multiplication understates it.

terms.definition: Pay increase tied to a published price index rather than to performance — Social Security's 2.5% raise for 2025 came directly from the CPI-W. Relocation uses the same arithmetic: moving a $60,000 salary to a city with a cost index of 130 against a base of 100 takes $78,000 to hold the same purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a transfer offer to a more expensive city is scored on running the index ratio, not on comparing the two base salaries.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: A restatement in which every income-statement line is divided by net sales and every balance-sheet line by total assets, turning all figures into percentages. Removing scale is what lets a single corner store be compared directly against a national chain or an industry average, a comparison raw dollar totals make impossible.
terms.whyItMatters: Benchmarking questions hand you two firms of wildly different size and ask which one controls cost of goods sold better.

terms.definition: The exposure of a bondholder to rate changes: when market rates rise, existing bonds paying the older lower rate fall in price, and longer maturities fall further.
terms.whyItMatters: It is why an investment roleplay calls long-term bonds risky for a client who may need the money early, despite the bonds being fully repaid at maturity.

terms.definition: Development instrument that collects ratings from four vantage points — self, manager, peers and direct reports, usually 8 to 12 raters in total — and reports where the self-rating and everyone else's diverge. A performance appraisal is single-source and administrative, feeding pay and promotion, which is exactly why these results are normally kept out of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on using development resources is scored on knowing this tool informs growth, and that folding it into a pay decision makes raters stop being honest.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: Cash generated by operating activities minus the capital expenditures needed to keep the asset base intact — what is genuinely available for dividends, debt repayment, or expansion after the business has paid to sustain itself, which is why it can be deeply negative in a year of record reported profit.
terms.whyItMatters: Valuation and dividend-capacity questions are answered from this figure rather than from net income, which ignores the equipment the firm had to replace.

terms.definition: A contract paying a fixed stream of income for a set term or for life, bought with a lump sum — insurance against outliving savings rather than an investment for growth.
terms.whyItMatters: Retirement roleplays raise it for a client who fears running out of money, and its trade-off is giving up access to the principal.

terms.definition: Earnings measured in what they buy rather than in dollars received: a 3% raise against 4% inflation is a cut of roughly 1%, since 1.03 divided by 1.04 comes to 0.99. The nominal number on the offer letter can rise every single year while this one falls, which is why a raise is judged against the inflation rate and not against last year's salary.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item giving a raise percentage and an inflation rate is asking for this comparison, and the trap answer is the one that calls any raise an improvement.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: Days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding minus days payables outstanding — the number of days a dollar stays trapped between paying a supplier and collecting from a customer. A negative result means customers finance the business, and shortening it frees cash without a single additional sale.
